Out-of-bounds read in the compact Theta sketch deserialization of Apache DataSketches C++ (repo: datasketches-cpp).

compact_theta_sketch::deserialize() and wrapped_compact_theta_sketch::wrap() read header fields before checking that the input was long enough. For the compressed format, the size check could be defeated by a 32-bit overflow, and two header fields that control decoding were not validated; this also affected deserialization from a stream. A crafted or truncated sketch could cause a read past the end of the input. In the compressed case the over-read can be large, and the bytes read can become part of the deserialized sketch. This can cause a crash (denial of service) and could expose adjacent memory contents.

This issue affects Apache DataSketches C++: from 3.1.0 before 5.3.0. Only applications that deserialize Theta sketches from untrusted sources are affected.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 5.3.0, which fixes this issue.

Out-of-bounds read in the VarOpt union deserialization of Apache DataSketches C++ (repo: datasketches-cpp).

var_opt_union::deserialize() read the 32-byte preamble of a non-empty union after checking that only 8 bytes were available, so a truncated serialized union could cause a read of up to 24 bytes past the end of the input. For such inputs, the size remaining for the embedded sketch was also computed by an unsigned subtraction that could wrap around, so the embedded sketch's own size checks no longer limited reads to the input. The bytes read can become part of the deserialized union's state. This can cause a crash (denial of service) and could expose adjacent memory contents.

This issue affects Apache DataSketches C++: from 2.0.0-incubating before 5.3.0. Only applications that deserialize VarOpt unions from untrusted sources are affected.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 5.3.0, which fixes this issue.

Out-of-bounds read and write in the CPC sketch deserialization of Apache DataSketches C++ (repo: datasketches-cpp).

A crafted serialized CPC sketch passed to cpc_sketch::deserialize(), from either a byte buffer or a stream, can cause the decompressor to read past the end of the compressed data, because the read position was only checked after decoding finished. In the hybrid flavor, it can also cause a write outside an internal heap buffer, because decoded row indices were not validated. Several other header fields and decoded values, including lg_k, were also not validated. This can corrupt heap memory, causing a crash and potentially enabling further exploitation.

This issue affects Apache DataSketches C++: from 2.0.0-incubating before 5.3.0. Only applications that deserialize CPC sketches from untrusted sources are affected.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 5.3.0, which fixes this issue.

The parser trusts the first payload byte of a debug frame as the message length (msg_length) and copies that many bytes into a fixed-size 17-byte stack buffer (debug_msg) via memcpy without performing any bounds checking.

### Summary
`PdfParser`'s `get_value()` can recurse without any limit and crash with an uncaught `RecursionError`. It is reachable through `Image.save(im, fp=<pdf>, format="PDF", append=True)` when the existing PDF file is attacker-controlled. This is the same class of bug as https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 (the /Prev trailer chain loop, fixed earlier this year), in the same file, but in two different functions that fix did not touch.

### Details
**`get_value()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`**

This is a classmethod that takes `max_nesting: int = -1` and has a guard:

```python
if max_nesting == 0:
    return None, None
```

Every recursive call (nested arrays, dictionaries, indirect object definitions) passes `max_nesting=max_nesting - 1`. Since the default and every call site start at -1, this only ever counts down further negative: -1, -2, -3, and so on. It never equals exactly 0, so the guard never runs. A PDF object with a value nested a few thousand levels deep is enough to hit Python's recursion limit. It does not even need a valid `/Pages` tree, since `read_pdf_info()` parses the `/Root` object's own dictionary first, before checking anything else.

This advisory reports a single vulnerability: an ineffective recursion-depth guard in `PdfParser.get_value()` (the sentinel  `-1`  default never reaches the `== 0` check). The mention of GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 is comparative context for an already-fixed, already-CVE'd bug in a different function — it is not a second vulnerability being reported. The three trigger paths (nested arrays/dicts/indirect objects) are not independently fixable; they share one root cause and one fix location in  get_value() .

### Steps to reproduce
Both PDFs below are plain text, built directly in Python, no PDF library needed.

```python
from PIL.PdfParser import PdfParser

def build_pdf(root):
    out = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4\n")
    offset = len(out)
    out += f"1 0 obj\n".encode()
    out += root
    out += b"\nendobj\n"
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    xref_offset = len(out)
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    out += b"trailer\n"
    out += f"<< /Size 2 /Root 1 0 R >>\n".encode()
    out += b"startxref\n"
    out += f"{xref_offset}\n".encode()
    out += b"%%EOF"
    return bytes(out)

bomb = b"[" * 3000 + b"]" * 3000
root = b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R /Bomb " + bomb + b" >>"
with open("nesting_bomb.pdf", "wb") as f:
    f.write(build_pdf(root))

PdfParser("nesting_bomb.pdf")     # raises RecursionError
```

Expected: a clean `PdfFormatError`.

Actual: raises a raw `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`.

### Impact
- Availability: an attacker who controls the content of a PDF file that an application later appends an image page to (`Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`) can crash that request with a RecursionError, using a file of a few hundred bytes.
- Confidentiality: none.
- Integrity: none.
- Pillow cannot open PDFs for reading through `Image.open()`. `PdfParser` is only reached through the append-mode save path, so the app has to be doing that specific thing (for example, stamping or watermarking an existing PDF) for this to matter.

cwe.name: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')

cves.summary:
``` ============================================================================ ReDoS in XbmImagePlugin: 512-byte file stalls Image.open() for minutes Location: src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in XbmImageFile._open() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 512-byte file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` spend about six minutes of processor time on one core before it gives up with `UnidentifiedImageError`. Anyone who can hand bytes to an application that opens images with Pillow's default settings can trigger this, for example through an upload form, a thumbnailer, or a service that checks whether a blob is an image. A few such files sent at once can tie up a typical pool of worker processes. The cause is the `xbm_head` regular expression in `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`, which `XbmImageFile._open()` (line 58) runs over the first 512 bytes of any stream whose prefix starts with `#define`. Several adjacent parts of the pattern can match the same characters. `[ \t]+` overlaps with `.*` in the width and height lines and with `[^_]*` in the optional hotspot lines, and `[\r\n]+` closing the hotspot group overlaps with the following `[\000-\377]*`. The header sets a run of k spaces after each `#define` and a run of k line terminators after `_y_hot`, then omits the `[]` after `_bits`. That forces Python's backtracking matcher to try every way of splitting those runs and rescan the remaining bytes each time. The cost grows roughly as k to the fifth power: k = 60 measured 375 s, while a well-formed XBM of the same size opens in about 40 ms. Because this happens before any format is identified, none of Pillow's size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb limits apply, and upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` repeats the cost on every chunk until the stream is identified. The only existing mitigation is passing a `formats=` allowlist that excludes `"XBM"`. The attached reproducer opens the same header with and without the trailing `[]`. The valid version opens as XBM in 52 ms. The broken version takes 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25, and the slow k = 60 case is not run. This is the same class of bug as CVE-2021-25292 in `PdfParser`, but in a different plugin and reachable from plain `Image.open()`. ## Details `XbmImageFile._open()` identifies an XBM file by running the module-level regex `xbm_head` over the first 512 bytes of the stream. The pattern has several adjacent quantifier pairs that can consume the same characters, followed by a `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` tail that rescans the rest of the buffer for every way of splitting them. A 512-byte input built to exercise all of them and then fail the final literal keeps `Image.open()` in `xbm_head.match()` for minutes before it raises `UnidentifiedImageError`. This 512-byte input (k = 60) takes 375 s of CPU in `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` with default settings, measured on the stock build at this commit: ```python k = 60 data = b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_width 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_height 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_x_hot 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_y_hot 1" + b"\r"*k data += b"_bits" # no "[]": the final literal never matches data += b"A" * (512 - len(data)) # pad to the 512 bytes _open() reads ``` Calling `XbmImagePlugin.xbm_head.match(data)` directly gives the same picture: k = 10 → 0.11 s, k = 15 → 0.76 s, k = 20 → 3.0 s, k = 25 → 8.5 s, k = 30 → 19.9 s (roughly ×27 per doubling of k, i.e. about k^4.7). A well-formed 512-byte XBM matches in 10 µs and opens and loads through `Image.open()` in ~40 ms including plugin import; the same k = 60 header with `_bits[]` present matches in 5 µs. The regex, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32`: ```python xbm_head = re.compile( rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` and the only call site, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58`: ```python def _open(self) -> None: … m = xbm_head.match(self.fp.read(512)) if not m: msg = "not a XBM file" raise SyntaxError(msg) ``` For a well-formed header (`#define im_width 8\n…static char im_bits[] = {`) each `[ \t]+` eats the single space, `.*`/`[^_]*` eat the identifier prefix, and `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` finds the literal on its first backward scan, so the match is linear. The crafted header diverges at every one of those points: - `[ \t]+.*_width` and `[ \t]+.*_height`: the run of k spaces after `#define` can be split between `[ \t]+` and `.*` in k ways, all leading to the same continuation. Factor k each. (The choice of `\r` terminators is incidental: the same header with `\n` terminators is equally slow.) - `[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot` and `[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot` inside the optional `hotspot` group: `[^_]*` also matches spaces, so the same k-way split exists twice more. Factor k each. These two lines are essential: without them the same input is rejected in about 10 ms. - `[\r\n]+` closing the `hotspot` group, followed by `)?` and `[\000-\377]*`: the run of k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1` can be divided between `[\r\n]+` and `[\000-\377]*` in k ways. Factor k. - `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]`: for every combination above, the engine swallows the remaining ~150 bytes of padding and walks back looking for `_bits[]`. The input contains `_bits` but never `[]`, so this always fails and every combination is visited. CPython's `re` is a backtracking engine without memoisation, so the total work is on the order of k^5 × (512 − header length) steps — about 10^11 for k = 60, consistent with the measured 375 s. The 512-byte read caps k (5k + ~60 ≤ 512), so the cost per `open()` is bounded, but the bound is minutes of CPU. The path is the default one. `Image.open()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3719`) reads a 16-byte prefix and offers it to every registered plugin's accept hook; `XbmImagePlugin._accept()` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:43`) returns true for anything whose left-stripped prefix starts with `#define`, and `_open()` then runs the regex. No size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb check can apply before this point because nothing has been parsed yet, and since the match ultimately fails the file is never identified, so the only outcome for the caller is `UnidentifiedImageError` after the delay. File name and extension are irrelevant because dispatch is by content. A `faulthandler` stack dump taken 20 s into the call shows the interpreter at `XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in _open` ← `ImageFile.py:154 in __init__` ← `Image.py:3699 in _open_core` ← `Image.py:3719 in open`. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:584`) amplifies this further: until the stream is identified it calls `Image.open()` on all accumulated data at every `feed()`, so an application feeding the stream in chunks pays the regex cost once per chunk (measured: k = 15 header fed in 8 chunks → 4.6 s versus 0.76 s for a single `open()`). ## Impact Anyone who can get 512 bytes in front of `Image.open()` — an upload endpoint, thumbnailer, or any service that uses Pillow to sniff whether a blob is an image — pins one CPU core of the handling process for roughly six minutes per request with the default plugin set and default limits. Nothing large is allocated and no `DecompressionBombWarning`/`Error` fires; application-side upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny, and `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` is never consulted because no image is ever identified. A handful of concurrent requests is enough to exhaust a typical worker pool. The per-call cost is bounded by the 512-byte header read, so this is a CPU-exhaustion denial of service of the handling process rather than an infinite loop. Applications that pass an explicit `formats=` allowlist to `Image.open()` that excludes `"XBM"` are not affected. This is the same bug class as CVE-2021-25292 (catastrophic backtracking in the `PdfParser` regexes, fixed in 8.1.1) and CVE-2021-23437 (`ImageColor.getrgb` ReDoS, fixed in 8.3.2), in a different plugin; unlike the PDF case it is reached from plain `Image.open()` on any byte stream. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the installed Pillow through the public `Image.open()` API and needs no rebuild. Each input is the 512-byte header from Details: four `#define` lines with k spaces after `#define`, lines ending in `\r`, k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1`, padding with `A` up to the 512 bytes that `_open()` reads. The only thing that changes between inputs is the tail: `_bits[]` (valid) or `_bits` (the final literal can never match). 1. **Control.** Opens the k = 60 header with the tail `_bits[]`. The regex matches on its first try and Pillow reports `XBM (1, 1)` in about 50 ms. This shows that the same bytes are only slow when the match has to fail. 2. **Attack.** Opens the header with the tail `_bits` at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25. Each one raises `UnidentifiedImageError`, after about 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s. The time grows polynomially, not linearly. The k = 60 input from Details, which takes about 6 minutes of CPU, is not run. Expected output on this commit: ``` control k=60 '_bits[]': XBM (1, 1) in 0.052s attack k=10 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.105s attack k=15 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.748s attack k=20 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 3.024s attack k=25 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 8.561s BUG ``` The script prints `BUG` only when all of these hold: - the control header opened as `XBM` in under 1 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 2 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 5 times as long as the k = 15 one, i.e. the cost grows super-linearly in k. Otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, every attack input is rejected at once, so the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch removes the overlap between `[ \t]+` and the quantifier that matches the identifier prefix in `xbm_head` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`), so the whitespace after `#define` can be consumed in exactly one way and the identifier cannot run across line terminators. ``` ============================================================================ Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs Location: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86 in MicImageFile.tell() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads `im.n_frames` can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with `save_all=True` to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it. The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. `MicImageFile` subclasses `TiffImageFile` and overrides `seek()` and `tell()` so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits `TiffImageFile.n_frames` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with `self._seek(self.tell() + 1)` until `_n_frames` is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress: - `MicImageFile.tell()` (`src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86`) returns the constant stream index. - `MicImageFile.seek()` calls `TiffImageFile._open()`, which resets `_n_frames` to `None`. As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. `Image.open()`, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds. ## Details `MicImageFile` (registered for `Image.open` whenever `olefile` is installed) subclasses `TiffImageFile` and redefines a "frame" as one OLE `*.ACI/Image` stream, overriding `seek()` and `tell()` accordingly. It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on `tell()` advancing as IFDs are loaded. `MicImageFile.tell()` returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside `n_frames`, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever. A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose `img0.ACI/Image` stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. `Image.open()` on it succeeds (format `MIC`, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating `im.n_frames` then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is ``` File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_frames ``` and instrumenting `_seek` shows it being called with `frame=1`, `tell()==0`, `_frame_pos==[8, 122]`, `_n_frames is None` on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give `n_frames == 3` in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives `n_frames == 1`. The loop, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`: ```python @property def n_frames(self) -> int: current_n_frames = self._n_frames if current_n_frames is None: current = self.tell() self._seek(len(self._frame_pos)) while self._n_frames is None: self._seek(self.tell() + 1) # 1219 self.seek(current) ``` and the overrides that break its progress assumption, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76`: ```python def seek(self, frame: int) -> None: … self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename) TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) # 82: resets _n_frames to None self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: return self.frame # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frame ``` For a plain TIFF, `_seek(k)` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1236`) loads IFDs up to `k`, appending each offset to `_frame_pos`, setting `_n_frames` when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private `__frame = k`; `TiffImageFile.tell()` returns `__frame`, so `self.tell() + 1` walks the chain to its end. For a MIC file, `Image.open` → `MicImageFile._open` sets `self._n_frames = len(self.images)` at line 69, but then calls `self.seek(0)` → `TiffImageFile._open` (line 82), which unconditionally sets `self._n_frames = None` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1203`) and `_seek(0)`s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so `_n_frames` stays `None` after open. `n_frames` then runs: `current = self.tell()` is `0` (the OLE index); `_seek(len(_frame_pos))` = `_seek(1)` loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also non-zero and not yet in `_frame_pos`, so `_n_frames` is still `None`. The `while` body computes `self.tell() + 1` = `0 + 1` and calls `_seek(1)` again; `len(_frame_pos)` is already 2, so nothing new is loaded — IFD 1 is re-read via `tag_v2.load` and `_setup()` and the state is unchanged. This repeats indefinitely; IFD 2 is never reached. Two chained IFDs are not enough (IFD 1's next pointer of 0 sets `_n_frames = 2` on the first `_seek(1)`); three or more are. `Tests/test_file_mic.py::test_n_frames` passes only because `hopper.mic`'s stream has a single IFD, so `_seek(0)` sets `_n_frames = 1` and the loop is never entered; the `len(self.images)` assignment at line 69 is only consumed by the initial `_seek_check(0)` and is overwritten before any caller can read `n_frames`. The file needs no particular extension (OLE magic; `FpxImagePlugin` rejects it on CLSID and `MicImagePlugin` accepts it), default limits do not intervene, memory does not grow, and no exception is raised, so only an external watchdog ends it. Preconditions: `olefile` installed (it is an optional dependency; without it the MIC plugin is not registered) and the application touching `n_frames` or a `save_all` path. `Image.open()` itself, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. This is the same class of tiny-file, pure-Python non-termination as CVE-2021-28676 (FLI) and CVE-2021-28677 (EPS), and like CVE-2019-19911 (FPX) it depends on `olefile`; it differs in not being reached by the default open/load path. The regression was introduced in `0b33a87b0d15` ("Replaced property methods for n_frames and is_animated with normal properties", 2020-04-13), first released in 7.2.0, which replaced `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property with the `_n_frames` attribute that `TiffImageFile._open` overwrites. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (with `olefile`, which is what registers the MIC plugin). It builds every input in code, writes each one to a temporary file named `x` with no extension (so Pillow identifies the format from its magic bytes), and opens it in a child Python process that runs `Image.open(path)` and prints `im.format` and `im.n_frames`. It builds two things in code: - `tiff(n)`: an `n`-page TIFF of 4×4 greyscale frames written by Pillow itself (`save_all=True`), so the IFDs are chained exactly as Pillow's own writer chains them. The last next-IFD pointer is 0. - `mic(stream)`: a minimal OLE2 compound file with a storage named `img0.ACI` that contains a stream named `Image`, which is the layout `MicImageFile._open` looks for. Sector 0 is the FAT and sector 1 is the directory. The stream starts at sector 2 and is padded to 4096 bytes, so the file doesn't need a mini-FAT. The result is 5632 bytes. It runs three inputs, each in its own child process with a hard 20-second kill: 1. control: the plain 3-page TIFF. Expected `TIFF n_frames = 3`. 2. control: a MIC wrapping a 1-page TIFF. Expected `MIC n_frames = 1`. 3. attack: the same MIC container wrapping the 3-page TIFF. The timeout is enforced by killing the child rather than by an in-process alarm, because a `TimeoutError` raised while `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` is parsing would be caught by its `except OSError` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:958`) and leave the IFD half-parsed instead of stopping the loop. The script prints `BUG` when both controls return and the attack child is still running after 20 seconds; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, the attack case prints `MIC n_frames = 1` and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch restores the OLE-level frame count after the embedded TIFF stream has been opened, so the inherited `n_frames` never enters its IFD-walking loop and `n_frames`/`seek()` agree on what a frame is. In `MicImageFile.seek`, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:82`, right after `TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self)`: ```diff TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame ``` Doing this in `seek()` restores the invariant on every seek, not only the first. The existing assignments at lines 69–70 of `_open` are kept: the initial `seek(0)` → `_seek_check(0)` reads `n_frames` before `TiffImageFile._open` has run, so they are still needed. Plain read-only `n_frames`/`is_animated` properties, as before 0b33a87b0, are no longer a drop-in option because `TiffImageFile._seek` assigns `self.is_animated`. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the attack file returns `n_frames == 1` immediately, a 2-IFD stream raises `EOFError` on `seek(1)` instead of `IndexError`, `save_all=True` to TIFF and PDF completes, and `Tests/test_file_mic.py` and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py` pass. No regression test is included, since one would need a new binary MIC fixture in `Tests/images`. The patch passed that check but has not been reviewed beyond it as the final form of the fix. Two things it leaves alone: it does not add the `_im` reset that `TiffImageFile.seek` performs after `_seek` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1229`), which matters when switching between OLE streams of different size or mode; and `TiffImageFile.n_frames` still advances via the overridable `tell()` rather than its private `__frame`, so making it iterate on `__frame` would protect any other subclass that redefines `tell()`. ## The patch Restore the OLE stream frame count in MicImageFile.seek() after TiffImageFile._open() resets it, so n_frames cannot loop forever Applies to `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. It passed the mechanical check — applied to a clean tree, rebuilt, the reproducer stopped firing — but a reviewer did not endorse it as the right fix. ```diff diff --git a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py index f8cf3a76f..2bb0109ce 100644 a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py @@ -81,6 +81,11 @@ class MicImageFile(TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile): TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: ``` ## The reproducer

Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # MicImageFile inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames, whose loop `self._seek(self.tell()+1)` # relies on tell() advancing; MicImageFile.tell() returns the OLE stream index (constant), # so a MIC file whose Image stream is a TIFF with >=3 chained IFDs makes im.n_frames spin forever. import io, struct, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os from PIL import Image def tiff(n): # n-page TIFF written by Pillow itself b = io.BytesIO(); fr = [Image.new("L", (4, 4), i) for i in range(n)] fr[0].save(b, "TIFF", save_all=True, append_images=fr[1:]); return b.getvalue() def mic(stream): # minimal OLE2 file: storage "img0.ACI" containing stream "Image" END, FREE, FATSECT = 0xFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFD data = stream.ljust(4096, b"\0"); n = len(data) // 512 fat = [FATSECT, END] + [3 + k for k in range(n - 1)] + [END]; fat += [FREE] * (128 - len(fat)) def entry(name, kind, child, start, size): raw = name.encode("utf-16-le") + b"\0\0" return raw.ljust(64, b"\0") + struct.pack(" {out}"); return hung c1 = run("control: 3-page TIFF, direct", tiff(3)) c2 = run("control: MIC around 1-page TIFF", mic(tiff(1))) bug = run("attack: MIC around 3-page TIFF", mic(tiff(3))) print("BUG" if bug and not c1 and not c2 else "OK") ```

``` ============================================================================ NULL dereference in ImagingExpand via rank filters on zero-size images Location: src/libImaging/Filter.c:79 in ImagingExpand() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Applying Pillow's median, minimum, maximum or rank filter to an image with zero width or zero height crashes the whole Python process instead of raising an error. Empty images like this are easy to produce with ordinary calls, for example a crop box whose left and right edges (or top and bottom edges) are equal, or the second page of a crafted multi-page image file. An attacker who can supply crop coordinates or an uploaded file to an application that runs one of these filters can kill its worker process. The effect is a crash only, with no memory disclosure or corruption. The fault is in `ImagingExpand()` in `src/libImaging/Filter.c`. This is the edge-padding step that `RankFilter.filter()` always runs through the core `expand()` method, so `MedianFilter`, `MinFilter` and `MaxFilter` go through it too. It fills the margin by copying the input's edge pixels, reading `imIn->image[y][0]` and rows `0` / `ysize-1`, and never checks that the input has any pixels. For an empty image, `ImagingAllocateArray` leaves the line pointers NULL, so the first read dereferences NULL and the process dies with SIGSEGV, in every mode. Zero-size images reach this point through public API alone: - `Image.crop()`, `ImageOps.crop()` and `Image.new()`; - a multi-page TIFF opened by path whose second IFD declares `ImageLength = 0`, on which `seek(1)` and `load()` succeed. Every other `ImageFilter` returns an empty image for the same inputs. The zero-height case has crashed since the original PIL import, and the zero-width case since Pillow 4.3.0. This is separate from the `margin == 0` fix in #9755: the path is the same, but here the degenerate value is the image size rather than the kernel size. It has the same shape as the zero-dimension `ImagingOffset` crash fixed under GHSA-f87v-9578-p47w. The attached reproducer shows a one-pixel-wide control crop filtering normally, while four empty crops passed through the rank filters are each killed by SIGSEGV. A patch that returns early in `ImagingExpand` for empty input is included. ## Details `ImagingExpand()` (`src/libImaging/Filter.c`), the edge-padding helper that `ImageFilter.RankFilter` runs before the actual rank filter, reads the first pixel of each input line without checking that the input has any pixels. For an image with width 0 or height 0 the line pointers are NULL, so `Image.filter()` with `MedianFilter`, `MinFilter`, `MaxFilter` or `RankFilter` kills the interpreter with SIGSEGV instead of returning or raising: ```python from PIL import Image, ImageFilter im = Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop((3, 0, 3, 10)) # size (0, 10); crop() accepts left == right im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3)) # SIGSEGV ``` Under gdb on the stock build the fault is at `ImagingExpand (imIn=…, margin=1) at src/libImaging/Filter.c:105` (the `EXPAND(UINT8, image8)` expansion), called from `_expand_image` at `src/_imaging.c:1151`, with `imIn->xsize = 0` and `imIn->image[0] = 0x0`. The same happens for every mode the rank filters accept (`L`, `RGB`, `RGBA`, `I`, `F`), and the core `expand(m)` method with `m >= 1` crashes the same way in any mode, including `P`. The same input through `BoxBlur`, `GaussianBlur`, `Kernel`, `ModeFilter` and `UnsharpMask` returns a `(0, 10)` image; a `(1, 10)` crop through `MedianFilter` also returns normally. The unchecked edge reads date from the PIL import (`9a640e315`, 2010, so every Pillow release): the zero-height case has crashed since then, and the zero-width case since `fd907fbdc` ("Fix 0-width and 0-height images other way", Pillow 4.3.0), which stopped backing zero-width images with a dummy block and left their row pointers NULL. It is adjacent to the `margin == 0` divide-by-zero fix in #9755 — same `expand()` → `ImagingExpand()` path, but the unhandled degenerate value here is the image size rather than the kernel size. The path: ```python # src/PIL/ImageFilter.py:111-116 RankFilter.filter (MedianFilter/MinFilter/MaxFilter subclass it) image = image.expand(self.size // 2) return image.rankfilter(self.size, self.rank) ``` `expand(m)` with `m > 0` is `ImagingExpand(self->image, m)` (`src/_imaging.c:1142-1151`). It validates only `margin`, allocates an output of `(xsize+2*margin) × (ysize+2*margin)` — which is non-empty, so the allocation succeeds — and then fills the margin by replicating edge pixels of the input: ```c // src/libImaging/Filter.c:70-101 imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); … #define EXPAND_LINE(type, image, yin, yout) \ { \ for (x = 0; x < margin; x++) { \ imOut->image[yout][x] = imIn->image[yin][0]; \ // line 79 } \ … \ for (x = 0; x < margin; x++) { \ imOut->image[yout][margin + imIn->xsize + x] = \ imIn->image[yin][imIn->xsize - 1]; \ // [-1] when xsize == 0 } \ } #define EXPAND(type, image) \ { \ for (y = 0; y < margin; y++) { \ EXPAND_LINE(type, image, 0, y); \ // line 0 of a 0-line image } \ … for (y = 0; y < margin; y++) { \ EXPAND_LINE(type, image, imIn->ysize - 1, margin + imIn->ysize + y); \ // line -1 when ysize == 0 } \ } ``` Why the line pointers are NULL: `ImagingNewPrologueSubtype` callocs the `im->image` pointer array (`src/libImaging/Storage.c:216`, at least one entry), and `ImagingAllocateArray` returns before assigning any of them for an empty image: ```c // src/libImaging/Storage.c:423-426 /* 0-width or 0-height image. ### Summary
`Image.merge()` checks the mode of every input band except band 0. If band 0 is a single-band `I` or `F` image, the native merge routine reads a pixel pointer that is NULL for those modes and the process crashes. The IPTC plugin reaches this from a plain `Image.open()` followed by a load, and IPTC has no magic-byte prefilter, so a crafted file with no recognizable header can drive it.

### Details
The validation loop skips band 0:

- `src/PIL/Image.py:3795` iterates `for band in bands[1:]` and checks mode and size only for those.

For an `I` or `F` image the 8-bit plane `image8` is NULL (only `image32` is set). `ImagingMerge` dereferences `bands[0]->image8[y]` for the multi-band output modes:

- `src/libImaging/Bands.c:302`, `:311`, `:321`

The IPTC loader builds the band list from an attacker-typed sub-image and passes it to merge with the sub-image at index 0:

- `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:156-160`
- `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:169` registers the opener with no accept function.

### PoC
```python
from PIL import Image

# Band 0 is a single-band "I" image: its image8 plane is NULL. merge() validates only
# bands[1:], so the native ImagingMerge dereferences the NULL plane for band 0.
band0 = Image.new("I", (4, 4))
Image.merge("RGB", [band0, Image.new("L", (4, 4)), Image.new("L", (4, 4))])
```

Run it:
```
$ python 02_poc.py
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

Observed on a source build of commit `3e2ab96`.

Under AddressSanitizer:

### Impact
NULL pointer dereference in a C extension. A crafted file opened and loaded through the IPTC path crashes the worker process. This is a hard crash, not a Python exception an application can catch.
